The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.

The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:92 — [P1, confidence 100] "const bookingAttendees = await prisma.booking.update({" — The database is committed before the external calendar update, so a provider failure leaves attendees persisted only locally and a retry rejects them as already present, making the cross-system inconsistency unrecoverable through this operation.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue in the code flow. Looking at addGuests.handler.ts, the code first updates the database with new attendees (line 92-108), then later calls eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking) (line 157) and sendAddGuestsEmails (line 161). If the calendar update fails, the attendees are already persisted in the database. On retry, the uniqueGuests filter (lines 68-72) will exclude these emails since they're already in booking.attendees, resulting in an empty uniqueGuests array and throwing 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' error. This creates an unrecoverable state where attendees exist locally but not in the external calendar, and the operation cannot be retried to fix it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:158 — [P1, confidence 100] "const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user);" — Calendar mutation is bound to the acting user even though attendees are authorized callers, so an attendee invocation attempts to update an organizer-owned event through the attendee's unrelated calendar credentials.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue. Looking at the code in addGuests.handler.ts, the handler allows three types of users to add guests: team admins/owners, the organizer, and attendees (lines 47-53). However, when updating the calendar event (lines 158-165), it uses `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` which gets the credentials of whoever is calling the API (could be an attendee), not the organizer's credentials. The EventManager is then initialized with these credentials and calls `updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)`. If an attendee calls this endpoint, their calendar credentials would be used to try to update the organizer's calendar event, which would fail or cause incorrect behavior since the attendee doesn't have access to the organizer's calendar.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts:5 — [P1, confidence 75] "guests: z.array(z.string().email())," — The API accepts an unbounded guest array that is materialized into database rows, translations, calendar attendees, and a single `Promise.all` email fan-out, creating a linear resource and provider-load cliff on a synchronous mutation.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue. Looking at the diff: 1) The schema at addGuests.schema.ts accepts `z.array(z.string().email())` with no length limit. 2) In addGuests.handler.ts, this array is used to create database rows via `createMany`, build attendee lists with translation lookups for each, update calendar attendees, and send emails via `Promise.all` in sendAddGuestsEmails. 3) In email-manager.ts, sendAddGuestsEmails iterates over all attendees sending individual emails. A malicious user could submit thousands of email addresses in a single request, causing database bloat, excessive API calls to calendar providers, and email spam - all in a synchronous mutation without rate limiting or bounds checking. This is a legitimate resource exhaustion vulnerability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:124 — [P2, confidence 100] "const evt: CalendarEvent = {" — The constructed event omits `team`, so `sendAddGuestsEmails` can never observe `calendarEvent.team?.members` and its team-member organizer-notification branch is unreachable for this integration path.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in addGuests.handler.ts line 124-145, the CalendarEvent object 'evt' is constructed without a 'team' property. In email-manager.ts lines 522-543, the sendAddGuestsEmails function checks 'calendarEvent.team?.members' to send OrganizerAddGuestsEmail to team members. Since 'evt' never has a 'team' property set, this branch will never execute for bookings that have team members. This is a real bug - team members won't receive notification emails when guests are added to team event bookings, even though the code in sendAddGuestsEmails is designed to handle this case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:167 — [P2, confidence 100] "try {" — Email delivery failures are swallowed after mutation with no retry/outbox state, allowing the operation to report success while permanently dropping all guest-change notifications.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in addGuests.handler.ts lines 167-170, email failures are caught and only logged with console.log('Error sending AddGuestsEmails'), then the function returns success with { message: 'Guests added' }. This means the database mutation succeeds (guests are added to the booking), but if email sending fails, users won't be notified and the operation still reports success. This is a real correctness issue - the operation claims success while silently dropping notifications. However, this pattern is common in many codebases where email is considered non-critical, and the guests ARE actually added to the booking. The finding overstates severity by calling it 'permanently dropping' when it's a design choice about error handling. Still, it's a legitimate concern that email failures are silently swallowed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts:5 — [P1, confidence 100] "guests: z.array(z.string().email())," — Server-side input validation omits non-empty, uniqueness, and size bounds, so direct API callers can submit duplicates or an unbounded guest batch despite the UI-only checks.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the server-side schema at addGuests.schema.ts only validates that guests is an array of email strings, but doesn't enforce non-empty, uniqueness, or size bounds. Looking at the handler (addGuests.handler.ts), there is some server-side validation: uniqueGuests filters out duplicates against existing attendees (lines 68-72), and throws an error if uniqueGuests.length === 0 (line 75). However, the schema itself doesn't prevent: 1) An empty array being submitted (though the handler would reject it), 2) Duplicate emails within the guests array itself (the handler only checks against existing attendees, not within the input), 3) Unbounded array size which could cause performance issues. The UI has a ZAddGuestsInputSchema with uniqueness validation via Set comparison, but this is client-side only. Direct API callers could submit duplicates within the array or very large arrays. This is a real validation gap.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:76 — [P1, confidence 75] "!booking.attendees.some((attendee) => guest === attendee.email)" — Existing-attendee and blacklist filtering is not case-normalized, so equivalent mixed-case email addresses bypass the intended duplicate/blacklist edge-case handling.

packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:168 — [P1, confidence 100] "await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests);" — Notifications use the unfiltered request rather than `uniqueGuests`, so existing or blacklisted addresses rejected from attendee creation are still emailed as though they were added.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in addGuests.handler.ts, the function filters guests to create `uniqueGuests` (line 68-72) which excludes existing attendees and blacklisted emails. However, at line 168, `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the original `guests` array from the input, not `uniqueGuests`. This means if a user tries to add an email that's already an attendee or is blacklisted, that email won't be added to the database (correct), but the email notification system will still receive those addresses and potentially send emails to them. This is a real bug - the notification should use `uniqueGuests` to only notify the guests that were actually added.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:158 — [P1, confidence 75] "const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user);" — The handler explicitly authorizes attendees and team admins but then attempts to update the organizer-owned destination calendar with the caller’s credentials, so adding a guest is operationally impossible for authorized non-organizers on providers that require the event owner’s credential.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real architectural issue. The code at line 158 gets credentials from ctx.user (the caller), but the EventManager.updateCalendarAttendees() is called to update the booking's calendar event. When an attendee or team admin (non-organizer) adds guests, they're using their own credentials to try to update a calendar event that belongs to the organizer. This would fail for calendar providers that require the event owner's credentials to modify the event. The authorization logic explicitly allows attendees and team admins to call this handler, but the calendar update operation uses the wrong user's credentials. This is a real functional bug where the feature would work for organizers but fail for other authorized users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:52 — [P1, confidence 75] "const isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find((attendee) => attendee.email === user.email);" — Treating any attendee as authorized lets a guest mutate the organizer's booking and invite arbitrary third parties who receive the private event details and join credentials.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real security concern. Looking at the code in addGuests.handler.ts lines 47-54, the authorization check allows any attendee (guest) of a booking to add more guests: `const isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find((attendee) => attendee.email === user.email)`. If `!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee` is false (meaning any of these is true), the user can proceed to add guests. This means any existing guest/attendee can add arbitrary new people to the booking, who would then receive the full event details including video call credentials. This is a legitimate authorization concern - typically only organizers should be able to modify attendee lists, not other attendees. The finding correctly identifies that this permission model may be too permissive, allowing guests to invite third parties to events they don't own.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts:5 — [P2, confidence 100] "guests: z.array(z.string().email())," — The authenticated mutation accepts an unbounded recipient array, enabling an authorized attendee to exhaust database/calendar/email resources and use the service for bulk invitation spam in one request.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real security concern. The schema at addGuests.schema.ts defines `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` with no maximum length constraint. Looking at the handler in addGuests.handler.ts, each guest triggers: 1) database writes to create attendees, 2) calendar API calls via eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(), and 3) email sends via sendAddGuestsEmails(). An authorized user (organizer, attendee, or team admin) could submit thousands of email addresses in a single request, causing resource exhaustion and potentially using the service for spam. This is a legitimate unbounded array vulnerability that could be exploited for abuse.
